function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

REPLACE MODE (mode='replace', default): find a unique string and replace it. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, path, old_string, new_string.
PATCH MODE (mode='patch'): apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes. REQUIRED PARAMETERS: mode, patch.

mode.description: Edit mode. 'replace' (default): requires path + old_string + new_string. 'patch': requires patch content only.

path.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. File path to edit.

old_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: REQUIRED when mode='replace'. Replacement text. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
REQUIRED when mode='patch'. V4A format patch content. Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: text_to_speech
function.description: Convert text to speech audio. Returns a MEDIA: path that the platform delivers as native audio. Compatible providers render as a voice bubble on Telegram; otherwise audio is sent as a regular attachment. In CLI mode, saves to ~/voice-memos/. Voice and provider are user-configured (built-in providers like edge/openai or custom command providers under tts.providers.<name>), not model-selected.

text.description: The text to convert to speech. Provider-specific character caps apply and are enforced automatically (OpenAI 4096, xAI 15000, MiniMax 10000, ElevenLabs 5k-40k depending on model); over-long input is truncated.

output_path.description: Optional custom file path to save the audio. Defaults to ~/.hermes/audio_cache/<timestamp>.mp3

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits. Auto-runs syntax checks on .py/.json/.yaml/.toml and other linted languages; only NEW errors introduced by this write are surfaced (pre-existing errors are filtered out).

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content": "     1|# Week 9: Days 57-63 Postpartum
     2|## Body: Maternal Recovery & Breastfeeding Maintenance
     3|
     4|By week 9 postpartum, your body has made significant healing progress. Most physical recovery from birth is complete, though you may still notice some lingering changes. Lochia (postpartum bleeding) should have stopped completely by now, and any perineal soreness or stitches should be fully healed.
     5|
     6|**Breastfeeding Maintenance**: At this stage, breastfeeding is typically well-established. Your milk supply has regulated to match your baby's demand, and you're likely feeling more confident with latch and positioning. However, it's common to experience fluctuations in supply perception around this time.
     7|
     8|> "constantly told my milk wasn't enough which honestly left me pretty scarred and anxious about supply" — Signal from r/breastfeeding
     9|
    10|If you're feeling anxious about your milk supply at 9 weeks, remember: breastmilk production operates on a supply-and-demand basis. As long as your baby is gaining weight appropriately, having adequate wet/dirty diapers, and seems satisfied after feeds, your supply is likely fine. Growth spurts can temporarily increase feeding frequency, which may make you feel like your supply has dipped—this is normal and usually resolves within a few days as your supply adjusts.
    11|
    12|**Physical Recovery & Self-Care**:
    13|- **Exercise**: If you had a vaginal delivery without complications, you can gradually return to more intense exercise now, but listen to your body. Start with low-impact activities and increase slowly.
    14|- **Pelvic Floor**: Continue pelvic floor exercises (Kegels) if recommended by your provider. Consider seeing a pelvic floor physical therapist if you have incontinence, pain, or pressure.
    15|- **Hair Loss**: You may notice increased hair shedding around now—this postpartum telogen effluvium is normal and peaks around 3-4 months before improving.
    16|- **Nutrition**: Continue eating nutrient-dense foods to support recovery and breastfeeding. Stay well-hydrated, especially if nursing.
    17|- **Breast Care**: Watch for signs of clogged ducts or mastitis, especially if you've started spacing feeds or baby is sleeping longer stretches.
    18|
    19|## Baby: Sleep Development & Routines
    20|
    21|At 9 weeks old, your baby is becoming more alert and interactive while still needing frequent feeds and plenty of sleep. This is a great time to begin gentle sleep shaping (not formal sleep training) to help establish healthy sleep habits.
    22|
    23|**Sleep Patterns**: 
    24|- Total sleep: 14-16 hours per day (though this varies widely)
    25|- Night sleep: May be starting to consolidate into longer stretches (4-6 hours is common, but still normal to wake every 2-3 hours)
    26|- Daytime naps: Typically 3-5 naps per day, ranging from 30 minutes to 2 hours
    27|- Sleep cues: Look for eye rubbing, yawning, fussiness, or decreased activity
    28|
    29|**Developmental Milestones**:
    30|- Social smiling in response to your voice or face
    31|- Cooing and making vowel sounds ("ah-goo", "ooh")
    32|- Following objects and people with eyes
    33|- Beginning to push up during tummy time (may lift chest off ground)
    34|- Grasping toys and bringing hands to mouth
    35|
    36|**Feeding**:
    37|- Breastfed babies: Usually nursing every 2-3 hours during day, possibly 1-3 night feeds
    38|- Formula-fed babies: Typically taking 4-5 oz every 3-4 hours
    39|- **Important**: Solids are NOT recommended yet. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends exclusive breastfeeding or formula feeding until around 6 months of age. Introducing solids too early increases risk of allergies, digestive issues, and doesn't provide nutritional benefits before baby's digestive system is ready.
    40|
    41|> "sleep dumpster fire" — Signal from r/sleeptrain
    42|
    43|If sleep feels challenging, focus on:
    44|- Consistent bedtime routine (bath, massage, book, feed)
    45|- Putting baby down drowsy but awake to practice self-soothing
    46|- Keeping night feeds calm and dark
    47|- Daytime exposure to natural light to help regulate circadian rhythms
    48|
    49|## Mental Health: Beyond the Baby Blues
    50|
    51|By week 9, the typical "baby blues" (mood swings, tearfulness, irritability) should have resolved. If you're still experiencing persistent sadness, anxiety, or overwhelm, it's important to recognize that this may be postpartum depression (PPD) or anxiety (PPA), which affects approximately 1 in 7 women and requires professional support.
    52|
    53|> "I'm feeling overwhelmed" — Signal from Quora
    54|> "don't want to mess this up" — Signal from Quora
    55|
    56|**Signs to watch for**:
    57|- Persistent sadness, hopelessness, or emptiness lasting more than 2 weeks
    58|- Loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed
    59|- Significant changes in appetite or sleep (beyond newborn-related changes)
    60|- Overwhelming anxiety or panic attacks
    61|- Intrusive thoughts about harming yourself or your baby
    62|- Feeling disconnected from your baby or having difficulty bonding
    63|- Thoughts that you're a "bad mother" or that your family would be better off without you
    64|
    65|**Coping Strategies**:
    66|- Prioritize sleep when possible—even short rests help
    67|- Continue accepting help with household tasks and baby care
    68|- Make time for brief activities that replenish you (shower, walk, phone call with friend)
    69|- Consider joining a postpartum support group (in-person or online)
    70|- Talk openly with your partner, family, or friends about how you're truly feeling
    71|- If symptoms persist or worsen, reach out to your healthcare provider—effective treatments are available
    72|
    73|## Partner Playbook: Deepening Connection & Support
    74|
    75|At 9 weeks postpartum, you're likely settling into new routines as a family. Your partner's continued support remains crucial for your recovery and the family's well-being.
    76|
    77|> "Partner involvement is an underserved gap" — Signal insight from dossier
    78|
    79|**Ways your partner can help**:
    80|- **Nighttime Teamwork**: Handle one wake-up completely (bring baby to you for nursing, then take over burping, diaper change, and resettling) so you can get longer uninterrupted sleep
    81|- **Daytime Relief**: Take baby for walks or wear them in a carrier while you nap, shower, or have uninterrupted time
    82|- **Feeding Support**: Bring water, snacks, and pillows during nursing sessions; handle burping and diaper changes after feeds
    83|- **Household Management**: Take ownership of specific ongoing tasks (laundry, dishes, grocery shopping) to reduce your mental load
    84|- **Emotional Check-ins**: Regularly ask "How are you *really* doing?" and listen without trying to fix things
    85|- **Baby Bonding**: Encourage skin-to-skin time, tummy time supervision, and interactive play (talking, singing, reading)
    86|- **Self-Care Facilitation**: Encourage and enable you to attend appointments, exercise, or social activities guilt-free
    87|- **Planning Ahead**: Help think through upcoming transitions (returning to work, childcare arrangements, etc.)
    88|
    89|**For partners**: Remember that supporting your partner's recovery isn't just about tasks—it's about creating a nurturing environment where she feels seen, valued, and cared for as she adjusts to motherhood.
    90|
    91|## Call Doctor? Red-Flag Table for Week 9
    92|
    93||| Symptom | Normal | When to Call |
    94|||---------|--------|--------------|
    95||| **Bleeding (Lochia)** | Should have stopped completely by 6-8 weeks postpartum | Any vaginal bleeding or spotting (could indicate infection, retained products, or hormonal issue) |
    96||| **Perineal/Abdominal Pain** | All birth-related soreness should be resolved | New or worsening pain, especially with fever, foul discharge, or urinary/bowel symptoms |
    97||| **Breast Health** | Comfortable breasts between feeds; occasional let-down sensation | Red, painful areas on breast (mastitis), fever with breast pain, cracked/bleeding nipples that won't heal, sudden drop in milk supply |
    98||| **Urinary/Bowel Function** | Normal urination and bowel movements without pain or leakage | Urinary incontinence, pain with urination, inability to control bowel movements, rectal bleeding, severe constipation |
    99||| **Emotional Health** | Mood stabilized; occasional stress or tiredness but able to enjoy baby | Persistent sadness >2 weeks, anxiety/panic attacks, intrusive thoughts, inability to bond with baby, thoughts of self-harm |
   100||| **Energy Levels** | Tired from broken sleep but functional between rests | Exhaustion that doesn't improve with rest, dizziness, rapid heartbeat, pale skin (could indicate anemia) |
   101||| **Baby's Feeding** | Steady weight gain, content after feeds, adequate wet/dirty diapers | Poor weight gain, lethargy, projectile vomiting, bloody/mucousy stools, signs of dehydration |
   102||| **Baby's Development** | Social smiling, cooing, following objects, beginning tummy time skills | Not responding to sounds or faces, not making eye contact, unusually floppy or stiff movements, not noticing hands |
   103|
   104|**Remember**: When in doubt about your physical or emotional health, or your baby's wellbeing, contact your provider. It's always better to check.
   105|
   106|---
   107|*This week's guidance is based on:*
   108|- *ACOG Committee Opinion No. 736: Optimizing Postpartum Care*
   109|- *ACOG Practice Bulletin: Postpartum Hemorrhage*
   110|- *AAP Policy Statement: Breastfeeding and the Use of Human Milk*
   111|- *AAP Recommendations on Infant Sleep Safety*
   112|- *WHO postnatal care guideline supported by 13 Cochrane Reviews*
   113|- *USPSTF Recommendation: Screening for Depression in Adults (includes postpartum)*
   114|- *Signal data from 83+ Reddit, Quora, and YouTube posts reflecting real maternal experiences*
   115|*Next week: We'll explore establishing more predictable routines, navigating growth spurts, and continuing to prioritize maternal mental health as you reach the 3-month postpartum mark.*", "total_lines": 114, "file_size": 9538, "truncated": false, "is_binary": false, "is_image": false}
